report:
**Conclusion: the claim is supported, not false**—with important limits.

A pivotal double-blind randomized trial assigned 120 patients aged 2–18 with drug-resistant Dravet syndrome to *add-on pharmaceutical cannabidiol* (20 mg/kg/day) or placebo for 14 weeks. Median monthly convulsive seizures fell from 12.4 to 5.9 with cannabidiol, versus 14.9 to 14.1 with placebo; the primary endpoint favored cannabidiol. Thus, the evidence directly supports a reduction in convulsive-seizure frequency, on average, in this population.  
https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1611618

A later randomized dose-ranging trial also evaluated adjunctive cannabidiol versus placebo for convulsive seizures in Dravet syndrome, providing independent trial evidence rather than relying on a single study.  
https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamaneurology/fullarticle/2762458

A systematic review/meta-analysis specifically of randomized placebo-controlled trials concluded that it evaluated cannabidiol’s efficacy and safety as adjunctive treatment in Dravet syndrome.  
https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40263-020-00708-6

This does **not** mean CBD cures Dravet syndrome, works for every child, or that retail/unregulated CBD products have the same evidence. Benefit must be balanced against adverse effects and drug interactions; the FDA label documents the controlled Dravet trial and its 2–18-year age range.  
https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2018/210365lbl.pdf
